messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi is an eighteen-year-old Black male of Ghanaian descent who recently completed his police training and is currently serving as a patrol officer in a mid-sized American city. He presented to an outpatient trauma clinic after being referred by his department's employee assistance program, having disclosed to a supervisor that he was struggling to function on shift. His PCL-5 score of 77 places him in a range consistent with severe posttraumatic stress, and the clinical picture that has emerged across his intake and first sessions is one of a young man whose earliest years left marks that have only deepened as his adult life has placed him, daily, in circumstances that resonate with them.

Kofi grew up in a household where violence between his parents was a recurring feature of domestic life. He describes his father as unpredictable — a man whose moods could shift without warning, whose silences in the evening were more frightening than his shouting, because the silence always came first. What Kofi remembers most vividly is not a single incident but a sequence of frozen images: his mother's face turned sideways against the kitchen wall, the particular angle of his own small body pressed into the corner behind the refrigerator, the way a glass sat on the counter before it was thrown. These memories do not return to him as a continuous narrative. They arrive as a series of still frames, each one complete and vivid in isolation, and when they surface he does not merely see them — he feels his body curl and contract, shoulders drawing inward, knees softening, as though he is once again that child folded into the corner of the kitchen. The grief that accompanies these moments is overwhelming and difficult for him to articulate; he has described it as a heaviness that settles across his chest and does not lift for hours.

In the months following his academy graduation and deployment to patrol duties, Kofi noticed that the world of his job seemed to activate something he had spent years learning to suppress. He is required, by the nature of his work, to enter unfamiliar buildings and respond to calls in neighbourhoods he does not know. He has come to dread these assignments, not because he doubts his training in any procedural sense, but because he is certain that in an unknown environment he cannot accurately read what is dangerous and what is not — and he has come to believe, with a quiet but absolute conviction, that his inability to read danger correctly means something terrible will happen. He has begun arriving early to briefings and walking the perimeter of buildings before entering, cataloguing exits and noting objects — a length of pipe left against a wall, a kitchen knife visible through a window, a belt draped over a chair — in a way that his colleagues have started to comment on. On one occasion a fellow officer clapped him on the shoulder from behind in the locker room, and Kofi's reaction — a sharp flinch, a wheeling around, hands raised — prompted enough concern that his supervisor initiated the referral.

On patrol, when a radio call goes quiet or a street falls suddenly still, Kofi feels a physical certainty that something violent is about to occur. He has also found himself watching members of the public with an intensity that has drawn complaints; when someone's behaviour strikes him as even mildly ambiguous, he cannot redirect his attention. He has received a formal caution about the tone of two interactions, and he is frightened that his career may be in jeopardy before it has properly begun.

What frightens Kofi most, in the privacy of his own thinking, is not any external threat but what he believes his symptoms say about him. He is convinced that his reactions — the flinching, the grief, the frozen images, the relentless scanning — mean that something in him has broken, that he is losing his grip on his own mind. He has come to feel that he cannot trust his own judgement or rely on himself to manage what comes at him. He arrived at the clinic hoping, above everything else, to be told that he is not going crazy — and afraid that the honest answer might confirm that he is.
